positions/believers-baptism/oneLine: Baptism is for those who personally repent and confess faith in Christ; it is an ordinance of obedience and public testimony to union with Christ in his death and resurrection, normally by immersion.
positions/believers-baptism/coreClaims/0: The New Testament order is hearing, believing, then being baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12; 18:8).
positions/believers-baptism/coreClaims/1: The church is a fellowship of professing believers; baptism marks entry into it.
positions/believers-baptism/coreClaims/2: Baptism signifies, and some say seals, a salvation already received by faith; it does not regenerate.
positions/believers-baptism/coreClaims/3: Immersion best displays burial and resurrection with Christ.
positions/believers-baptism/origin: Anticipated by the Anabaptists (1525); Baptist churches founded by John Smyth (Amsterdam, 1609) and Thomas Helwys (London, 1612); Particular Baptists (c.1638) adopted immersion c.1641 and confessed it in the London Confessions (1644, 1689).
positions/believers-baptism/strongestArg: It follows the explicit pattern and commands of the New Testament.
It guards the church as a community of conscious disciples and resists nominal Christianity.
Even the paedobaptist Karl Barth judged infant baptism a "wound" in the church’s practice.
positions/believers-baptism/strongestObj: Paedobaptists: it severs the continuity of the covenant and excludes children from the visible people of God.
Sacramentalists: it turns God’s act into a human act of testimony.
Rebaptising those baptised as infants denies "one baptism".
positions/believers-baptism/responses/0: Credobaptists answer that the new covenant is a covenant of the Spirit, entered personally by faith.
positions/believers-baptism/responses/1: They regard infant baptism as no baptism, so believers’ baptism is not a re-baptism.
positions/believers-baptism/consequences: Generated the global Baptist family and is the practice of most Pentecostal and independent churches.
Linked historically with religious liberty and church-state separation.
positions/baptismal-regeneration/oneLine: In baptism God himself, through the water joined to his Word and the Spirit, gives new birth, forgives sins and unites the baptised to Christ; baptism is normatively necessary for salvation.
positions/baptismal-regeneration/coreCla: Scripture attributes salvation to baptism: "born of water and the Spirit", "washing of regeneration", "baptism now saves you".
Baptism is God’s work, not merely a human testimony.
Faith receives what baptism gives; in infants God creates faith or it is supplied by the Church.
Catholic and Orthodox teaching adds that baptism imprints an indelible character; God is not bound by the sacrament in extraordinary cases (baptism of blood and desire).
positions/baptismal-regeneration/origin: Universal patristic teaching (Justin, Tertullian, Cyril of Jerusalem, Augustine); defined by Florence (1439) and Trent (Session VII, 1547); confessed by Lutherans (Small Catechism, 1529); taught in a believers’-baptism form by the Stone-Campbell Churches of Christ.
positions/baptismal-regeneration/stronge: It takes at face value the strongest New Testament statements about baptism.
It reflects the consensus of the early church.
It roots assurance in God’s objective promise: "I am baptised".
Evangelical critics: it makes salvation depend on a rite rather than faith (Eph 2:8-9), and the thief on the cross was saved unbaptised.
Many baptised people show no sign of new life.
Reformed: it ties the Spirit’s freedom to the moment of administration.
positions/baptismal-regeneration/respons: Sacramentalists answer that baptism is the gospel promise in action, received by faith, not a work.
They note that God can save outside baptism, but has bound us to it; the baptised can fall away.
positions/baptismal-regeneration/consequ: Shapes liturgy, emergency baptism and pastoral practice (e.g. baptism of dying infants).
Divides Restorationist Churches of Christ from Baptists.
positions/mode-immersion/oneLine: Baptism should be (or is best) administered by immersing the whole body in water, enacting burial and resurrection with Christ; in Eastern churches by a threefold immersion in the name of each divine Person.
positions/mode-immersion/coreClaims/0: Baptizō means to dip or plunge.
positions/mode-immersion/coreClaims/1: Romans 6:4 and Colossians 2:12 picture burial and rising.
positions/mode-immersion/coreClaims/2: New Testament baptisms took place "in" rivers with candidates coming "up out of the water".
positions/mode-immersion/coreClaims/3: Eastern practice: triple immersion, even of infants; many Baptists hold immersion essential to valid baptism.
positions/mode-immersion/origin: The early church’s normal practice (Didache, Hippolytus, Cyril of Jerusalem); preserved in Eastern and Oriental churches; restored in the West by Baptists (c.1641), Churches of Christ, Brethren (Dunkers, trine immersion), Pentecostals; permitted and encouraged in Catholic adult initiation since 1972.
positions/mode-immersion/strongestArgume: It best fits the meaning of the word and the symbolism of death and resurrection.
It is attested as the norm in the early church in East and West.
Its dramatic symbolism aids teaching and memory.
positions/mode-immersion/strongestObject: Affusion and aspersion advocates: the Didache permitted pouring, and the meaning of baptism does not depend on quantity of water.
Some New Testament baptisms (the jailer at night, 3,000 at Pentecost) may not have allowed immersion.
Making mode essential divides Christians unnecessarily.
positions/mode-immersion/responses/0: Immersionists answer that Jerusalem had many pools (mikvaot) and that the Didache’s exception proves the rule.
positions/mode-immersion/responses/1: Many now hold immersion preferable without denying the validity of other modes.
positions/mode-immersion/consequences/0: Baptistery and river-baptism traditions; Orthodox insistence on triple immersion affects recognition of Western baptisms in some cases.
positions/mode-affusion/oneLine: Baptism by pouring water over the head (often three times) is a valid and ancient mode, symbolising the outpouring of the Spirit and cleansing.
positions/mode-affusion/coreClaims/0: The Didache explicitly permits pouring water three times when immersion is impractical.
positions/mode-affusion/coreClaims/1: Pouring signifies the Spirit "poured out" (Acts 2:17-18; Titus 3:5-6).
positions/mode-affusion/coreClaims/2: The essence of baptism is washing with water in the triune name, not the quantity of water.
positions/mode-affusion/coreClaims/3: Many Mennonites baptise adult believers by pouring.
positions/mode-affusion/origin: Attested in the Didache (c.100) and early catacomb art showing water poured over a candidate standing in a font; became the normal Latin practice in the later Middle Ages and remains the most common Catholic mode.
positions/mode-affusion/strongestArgumen: It is explicitly authorised in the earliest church order outside the New Testament.
It ties baptism to the gift of the Spirit.
It is practical in all climates and for the sick.
positions/mode-affusion/strongestObjecti: Immersionists: it loses the burial-resurrection symbolism of Romans 6.
The Didache treats it as an exception, not the norm.
The Eastern churches regard it as irregular except in emergencies.
positions/mode-affusion/responses/0: Defenders reply that Scripture uses many images of baptism (washing, pouring, clothing, sealing).
positions/mode-affusion/responses/1: Early iconography often shows candidates standing in water with water poured over them — a combination of modes.
positions/mode-affusion/consequences/0: Normal practice of Western Catholicism and many Protestant churches.
positions/mode-aspersion/oneLine: Baptism by sprinkling water is valid, recalling the sprinkling of purification and of the blood of the covenant.
positions/mode-aspersion/coreClaims/0: Old Testament purification by sprinkling foreshadows baptismal cleansing.
positions/mode-aspersion/coreClaims/1: Hebrews speaks of hearts "sprinkled" and bodies "washed".
positions/mode-aspersion/coreClaims/2: Validity rests on the Word and the triune name, not on the amount of water.
positions/mode-aspersion/coreClaims/3: Historically used for the sick ("clinical baptism", as of Novatian c.250).
positions/mode-aspersion/origin: Clinical baptism of the sick is attested by c.250 (Cornelius on Novatian, in Eusebius HE 6.43), accepted with reservations by Cyprian; sprinkling became common in Reformed, Presbyterian and Methodist infant baptism.
positions/mode-aspersion/strongestArgume: Scripture links sprinkling with covenant cleansing (Ezek 36:25; Heb 10:22).
Cyprian defended the validity of clinical baptism by sprinkling.
It is gentle and practical for infants.
positions/mode-aspersion/strongestObject: Clinical baptism was regarded as irregular; Novatian’s ordination was questioned partly for this reason.
Eastern churches reject it except in necessity.
positions/mode-aspersion/responses/0: Defenders answer that the New Testament uses baptizō for ritual washings (Mark 7:4; Luke 11:38) not requiring full immersion.
positions/mode-aspersion/responses/1: Calvin held the mode a matter of indifference to be decided by the church according to climate and custom (Institutes IV.15.19).
positions/mode-aspersion/consequences/0: Typical of Reformed and Methodist infant baptism in Europe and North America.
positions/anabaptist-baptism/oneLine: Baptism is the visible covenant of a good conscience with God and the church, given only to those who have repented and believed, and marks entry into a disciplined, separated community of disciples ready to suffer.
positions/anabaptist-baptism/coreClaims/: Infant baptism is not baptism, since faith and repentance must precede; hence the name "Anabaptist" (re-baptiser) was rejected by those so called.
Baptism is a pledge (Bundeszeichen) to walk in obedience and to accept fraternal admonition and the ban.
Three baptisms: of the Spirit (inward), of water (outward), and of blood (martyrdom) — as Hans Hut and Hubmaier taught.
The church is a voluntary community separate from state coercion.
positions/anabaptist-baptism/origin: Swiss Brethren in Zurich (Grebel, Manz, Blaurock, 21 January 1525), Hubmaier at Waldshut (1525), the Schleitheim Confession (1527), Pilgram Marpeck, Hutterites (1528) and Menno Simons (from 1536).
positions/anabaptist-baptism/strongestAr: It restores the New Testament order and the church as a community of committed disciples.
It refuses state-enforced religion and coerced faith, anticipating religious liberty.
Its witness was sealed by thousands of martyrs.
positions/anabaptist-baptism/strongestOb: Magisterial Reformers and Catholics: rebaptism repeats the unrepeatable sacrament and is sedition (Code of Justinian revived at Speyer, 1529).
Its separatism withdraws Christians from public responsibility.
Münster (1534-35) showed, critics said, its revolutionary potential (though most Anabaptists were pacifist).
positions/anabaptist-baptism/responses/0: Anabaptists replied that Christ’s kingdom is not of this world and faith cannot be coerced.
positions/anabaptist-baptism/responses/1: Mennonite historians distinguish the pacifist mainstream from Münsterite apocalypticism.
positions/anabaptist-baptism/consequence: Thousands executed by drowning, burning and beheading; migrations to Moravia, the Netherlands, Prussia, Russia and the Americas.
Source of Mennonite, Amish, Hutterite and (indirectly) Baptist traditions.
positions/oneness-jesus-name-baptism/one: Valid baptism is by immersion "in the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 2:38), because Jesus is the one name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; baptism (with Spirit baptism evidenced by tongues) is part of the new birth.
positions/oneness-jesus-name-baptism/cor: The apostles consistently baptised in the name of Jesus (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5).
Matthew 28:19 commands baptism into "the name" (singular), which is Jesus.
God is one, revealed as Father, Son and Spirit as modes or manifestations, not three persons (outside historic Nicene orthodoxy).
Many Oneness churches teach that repentance, water baptism in Jesus’ name and Spirit baptism with tongues together constitute salvation.
positions/oneness-jesus-name-baptism/ori: Arose at the Arroyo Seco world-wide camp meeting near Los Angeles (1913) after R. E. McAlister’s remark on apostolic baptism; Frank Ewart and Glenn Cook re-baptised in Jesus’ name (April 1914); the "New Issue" split the Assemblies of God (1916); United Pentecostal Church International formed 1945.
positions/oneness-jesus-name-baptism/str: It follows the actual formula recorded in Acts.
It emphasises the full deity of Jesus and the oneness of God.
It treats the apostolic pattern in Acts as normative for today.
Trinitarian Christians: it rests on a modalist doctrine of God rejected since the 3rd century, placing it outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
"In the name of Jesus" in Acts likely denotes Christian (as opposed to John’s) baptism, not a liturgical formula excluding Matthew 28:19.
Requiring tongues and a specific formula for salvation unchurches most Christians.
positions/oneness-jesus-name-baptism/res: Oneness theologians answer that they confess Father, Son and Spirit, but as one person revealed in Jesus.
They argue the Didache and Matthew’s triadic formula are fulfilled, not contradicted, by the name of Jesus.
positions/oneness-jesus-name-baptism/con: A distinct Pentecostal family of perhaps 20-30 million worldwide (estimates vary), strong in the Americas, Ethiopia ("Jesus Only" churches) and Asia.
